catalog_quote: [p.11, §2.0] Gangte has thirty inventory phonemes. They can be divided into two groups - segmental and suprasegmental phonemes. Vowels and consonants are segmental phonemes. Out of twenty-eight segmental phonemes, six are vowels and twenty-two are consonant phonemes. The suprasegmental phonemes are tones, that is, level and falling tones. The thirty phonemes can be classified as: a] Segmental phonemes — Vowels — Consonants b] Suprasegmental phonemes - Tones — Mid tone — Low tone [...] [p.43, §2.4 Tones] As in other Tibeto-Burman languages, Gangte has a tonal system in the sense that pitch variation affects the meaning of the word by level or by falling etc. "When a syllable is associated with a particular pitch level such as high, mid, low etc., and the pitch distinguishes the meanings of words, then the pitch is called tone and the language which has tone is a tone language. new_statements.rule_in_words: Gangte is described as a tone language with two lexical tones (mid vs low), contrasted on monosyllables. The grammar makes no statement of any kind about word stress or prominence: no stress section, no stress marks on the mono- to quadrisyllabic words listed under syllable division (pp. 41-43), and the words 'stress'/'accent' do not occur in the thesis.
new_statements.exceptions: None; note the ch.1 (p.1) and §2.0 (p.11) summaries say 'level and falling' tones while §2.4 and ch.9 name them 'mid' and 'low' — an internal inconsistency in tone labels, not about stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Tone is presented as a lexical property of the (monosyllabic) word; 'intonation' is invoked once (ch. 7, yes/no questions) at sentence level. Nothing on stress at word or phrase level, citation forms only.
new_statements.identity_note: Devi 2010 describes the Gangte of Chienkongpang (Chengkonpang) village, Churachandpur district, Manipur; she states the language has no dialectal variation (Wikipedia/Ethnologue agree). Alternate name Gante/Rante. Same languoid as gang1266; no dialect glottocode involved. Data are Roman-script phonemic transcriptions; the ABBYY scanned of the PDF garbles some IPA symbols (e.g. ŋ rendered as 'g'/'q'/'rj'), so quotes were checked against the page image text layer only, not re-scanned.

sources.note: Chapter II Phonology (pp. 11-45) covers vowels, consonants, syllable (structure, pattern, division, pp. 39-42) and tone (2.4, pp. 42-45): Gangte is tonal with two lexical tones, mid (marked) vs low (unmarked), established by monosyllabic minimal pairs. The words 'stress', 'accent' and 'prominence' do not occur anywhere in the thesis (scanned text of all 14 bitstreams a full-text search for stress/accent); polysyllabic words in the syllable-division lists carry no prominence marks.
